cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, is writing to God's people in Rome (Romans 1:1, 7). He's just told them sin shall not be their master, because they're not under law, but under grace (Romans 6:14). So he asks the question somebody was bound to ask: "Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace?"

cards.question: Paul asks if we should keep sinning since we're under grace and not under law. What's his answer?

cards.text: Friend, that's like me telling a baker every burnt batch is forgiven, and he cranks every oven to MAXIMUM just to celebrate. Then Paul explains with a picture he says they should already know: slaves and masters.

cards.question: In Paul's picture of slaves and masters, who does he say you're a slave to?

answers.text: The one you were born under

cards.question: Paul says that besides being a slave to sin or to obedience, there's a third option: offering yourself to no master at all.
Paul says each master takes you somewhere. You're a slave either to sin leading to ___, or to obedience leading to ___.

cards.text: Then Paul stops and says, "But thanks be to God." These folks in Rome once were slaves to sin, but that's not where their story stayed.

cards.question: The believers in Rome were once slaves to sin. What does Paul thank God that they did?

answers.text: Kept every part of the law
Worked to earn their own freedom

cards.question: Paul says that once the believers in Rome were set free from sin, they had no master at all.

cards.text: Set free from sin, they've become slaves to righteousness, and then Paul says, "I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh." I respect a man who keeps it simple, friend, because when I explain my oven I need my MUSTACHE for hand motions.

cards.question: Paul says the believers used to offer the parts of their body in slavery to impurity. What does he tell them to do with those same parts now?

answers.text: Offer them in slavery to righteousness
Keep them out of all service
Offer them back to the law

cards.question: Impurity led them into escalating wickedness. But Paul says slavery to righteousness leads to ___.

cards.text: Then Paul looks back: when they were slaves to sin, they were free of obligation to righteousness. That's me in the junk drawer bragging I had no deadlines, when really nobody needed me for ANYTHING.

cards.question: Paul asks what fruit they reaped back then from the things they're now ashamed of. What does he say the outcome of those things is?

cards.text: Then come two words I'd stamp on every cookie I own: but now. Paul says they've been set free from sin and have become slaves to God, and the fruit they reap leads to holiness.

cards.question: Paul says that for those who've been set free from sin and become slaves to God, the outcome is the same as it was before.

cards.text: Then Paul lands the whole thing with one line, and it starts on payday. Sin hands out a paycheck, friend, and trust me, you do NOT want to open that envelope.

cards.question: Paul puts what sin pays next to what God gives: the wages of sin is ___, but the ___ of God is eternal life.
Paul says eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord is something you earn, the same way you earn wages.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 7 quotes "But thanks be to God.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The right answer "Certainly not" is Paul's own formal wording. The wrong answers "Only now and then" and "Only the small ones" are casual and flippant. The right answer stands out by tone, and the wrong answers read as close to silly.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The joke makes a baker the one being laughed at: he cranks every oven to MAXIMUM to celebrate being forgiven. Papa Dorin should be the target himself, for example by being the stamper tempted to do it.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself.

findings.problem: In Romans 6:19, Paul uses human terms because his readers are weak. Papa Dorin's comparison is him needing his mustache for hand motions when he explains his oven. That isn't the same action, and it doesn't click as a reason to respect someone who keeps it simple. A stranger would say "huh?"

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "Impurity led them into escalating wickedness" adds a cause-and-effect link the text doesn't state. Romans 6:19 lists impurity and escalating wickedness side by side, as two things they offered their bodies in slavery to.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The joke adds a new detail to the backstory: Papa Dorin bragging in the junk drawer that he had no deadlines. The backstory says that in the drawer "He didn't talk much. He didn't joke at all." Jokes may make up small moments around his bakery, not new drawer history.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.
